red.focus: Read legal words in the system that gives them force
red.summary: A legal text cannot be interpreted without knowing what kind of text it is and who made it authoritative. Learn why the same words can have different legal effects in a statute, contract, or treaty.
checklist: I can identify the legal status of a text
I can begin with words in their relevant context
I can separate ordinary language from legally defined terms

sections.title: Text and Source Are Different Questions
sections.body_md: The words 'must deliver' may appear in a statute, a contract, or a polite email. Their legal significance depends first on the source. Legislation may impose a public duty, a valid contract may create an obligation between parties, and an email may be evidence without creating any legal duty. Before interpreting disputed words, determine whether the document has legal force in the relevant jurisdiction and what law governs it. Context begins with authority, not with a dictionary.

sections.title: Read the Whole Sentence
sections.body_md: A rule says, 'Vehicles may enter the park except during maintenance.' Is entry permitted during maintenance? No: the exception changes the effect of the general permission. Quoting only the first clause would be misleading. A legal interpretation begins with the actual wording and reads qualifications, definitions and neighboring provisions together. This is straightforward language discipline, but its consequences can be serious when an omitted phrase affects liberty, money or access to a home.

sections.title: Definitions Can Change Familiar Words
sections.body_md: A statute may define 'vehicle' to include a bicycle even if everyday speakers use the word differently. A contract may define 'business day' by reference to a particular holiday calendar. The interpreter must identify whether a legally controlling definition applies before assuming ordinary meaning. If no such definition exists, language and context still matter. The beginner's method is simple: source, exact text, definitions, neighboring provisions, and the concrete dispute requiring interpretation.

yellow.focus: Distinguish ordinary meaning from contextual and purposive interpretation
yellow.summary: Build on textual reading to analyze how structure and purpose can clarify ambiguity. Learn why the correct approach depends on the legal system and instrument involved.
checklist: I can read a clause within its wider scheme
I can identify a relevant purpose without replacing the text
I can compare statutory and contractual contexts

sections.title: Meaning Comes From Structure
sections.body_md: A statute grants an agency power to inspect 'commercial premises' and elsewhere defines that term. The interpreter must read both provisions, not select a dictionary entry in isolation. Surrounding sections may distinguish homes, shops and temporary locations. Legal interpretation asks what meaning the legislature's chosen words bear in that context. An apparent ambiguity can disappear when the provision is read as part of the whole enacted scheme.

sections.title: Purpose Helps but Does Not Erase Words
sections.body_md: A consumer-protection statute may seek to prevent misleading sales practices. That purpose can inform how a disputed phrase is understood, but a court must still respect the language and limits enacted under its legal method. It cannot simply write a new rule because greater protection seems desirable. Different jurisdictions give different weight to preparatory materials and purpose. A careful explanation identifies the interpretive source and the exact textual uncertainty it helps resolve.

sections.title: Contracts Have Their Own Context
sections.body_md: A shipping agreement may use 'delivery' to mean arrival at a warehouse rather than receipt by the buyer. Definitions, related clauses, commercial setting and applicable contract doctrine can clarify the word. The court may examine certain surrounding circumstances under the governing law while restricting others. This is not identical to statutory interpretation, because contractual authority and party arrangements differ from legislative power. The analyst should identify which interpretive rules govern before borrowing a method from another context.

orange.focus: Apply treaty interpretation as a distinct legal method
orange.summary: Use the Vienna Convention framework to analyze the interpretation of treaty language in good faith. Distinguish the general rule from supplementary means and multilingual authenticity.
checklist: I can identify the components of Article 31 treaty interpretation
I can explain when Article 32 supplementary means are used
I can recognize issues raised by multiple authentic languages

sections.title: The General Treaty Rule
sections.body_md: Article 31 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties directs good-faith interpretation by ordinary meaning in context and in light of a treaty's object and purpose. This is a unified inquiry rather than a rule to choose whichever element produces a preferred result. Relevant context includes the text, preamble and annexes, along with specified related instruments. A lawyer should identify the treaty, parties, authenticated language and relevant provision before applying the framework. Treaty interpretation cannot simply be replaced with domestic statute-construction slogans.
sections.audio_script: Article 31 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties directs good-faith interpretation by ordinary meaning in context and in light of a treaty's object and purpose. This is a unified inquiry rather than a rule to choose whichever element produces a preferred result. Relevant context includes the text, preamble and annexes, along with specified related instruments. A lawyer should identify the treaty, parties, authenticated language and relevant provision before applying the framework. Treaty interpretation cannot simply be replaced with domestic statute-construction slogans.

sections.title: Supplementary Materials Have a Role
sections.body_md: Article 32 permits supplementary means, including preparatory work and circumstances of conclusion, to confirm an Article 31 reading or address ambiguity, obscurity or a manifestly unreasonable result. The provision does not license selective quotation from diplomatic history to override an otherwise defensible treaty interpretation. A rigorous analysis records what the supplementary materials actually show and how they relate to the text. Subsequent agreements and practice may also matter under Article 31's distinct rules.

sections.title: More Than One Authentic Language
sections.body_md: Some treaties are authentic in several languages. Article 33 addresses their status and methods of reconciling differences. A translation made for convenience is not necessarily an authentic treaty text. If equally authoritative versions diverge, the interpreter must use the relevant treaty rules, not assume the English version always wins. This matters when a word affecting jurisdiction or human rights has different shades of meaning across languages. Comparative legal competence includes knowing when translation itself is a contested legal question.

black.focus: Critique interpretive authority across institutional traditions
black.summary: At doctoral depth, analyze why textual fidelity and legitimate institutional change can pull in different directions. Compare judicial construction, negotiated meaning and contested religious legal interpretation without treating them as interchangeable.
checklist: I can explain institutional limits on interpretive creativity
I can compare treaty and domestic legal interpretation transparently
I can evaluate plural interpretations with source and community accountability

sections.title: The Interpreter Is Not the Author
sections.body_md: A statute's interpreter, treaty tribunal or private arbitrator may have a different mandate from the body that created the norm. Their power to develop meaning must be justified under the relevant legal system. Excessive rigidity can conceal genuine textual ambiguity, while unconstrained purposive interpretation can replace authorized choices with a decision maker's preferences. A doctoral theory should identify which interpretive moves positive law permits and which arguments instead seek legal reform. The distinction is crucial when rights and coercive power are at stake.

sections.title: Sacred Text and State Law Are Distinct
sections.body_md: Religious traditions may have developed sophisticated interpretive methods involving language, transmission, commentary and legal reasoning. Their use as enforceable state law depends on the particular constitutional and institutional arrangement, as well as diversity within the tradition. It is inaccurate to assume a sacred text always operates like a statute or that a religious community has only one authoritative interpreter. Comparative analysis should describe internal methods respectfully, distinguish theological from positive legal authority, and examine the rights of affected persons.

sections.title: Interpretation Needs Accountability
sections.body_md: A community may debate a text's meaning while state officials enforce one interpretation coercively. That creates questions of participation, legal notice, equality and review. A doctoral proposal must consider who can contest interpretation, what evidence is treated as authoritative, and how minority perspectives are protected. No interpretive method is simply a technical trick; it allocates power over people's relationships and freedoms. Masterful legal interpretation combines precision about sources with responsibility for human consequences.
